newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Kock trial confirms apartheid's most sordid side.
newsitem.headline: De Kock trial confirms apartheid's most sordid side.

text.p: After Eugene de Kock, white South Africans can no longer ignore the most sordid side of their apartheid past, however reluctant some may be to face the facts.

The trial of the state death-squad assassin, sentenced to more than 200 years in jail on Wednesday for murder and scores of other crimes, has shed so much light on the brutal excesses of the old order that not even the diehard can shield their eyes from the glare.
It has also sharpened the debate over how much ordinary whites knew, and who should share the blame.

De Kock and other apartheid servants, in a tide of confession prompted not by remorse but by self-interest, have now proved the state approved horrific torture and had opponents and innocent civilians eliminated.

"The tidal wave of the past is now so overwhelming, so compelling and so horrific that surely no one can ignore it any longer," John Battersby, editor of the influential Sunday Independent, wrote in his newspaper.
"If there was ever an excuse for not knowing what was happening, that has now been removed."
Many people -- blacks, liberal whites and most of the outside world -- have long assumed the white regime killed, tortured, terrorised, and covertly set black against black.
But a core of ordinary white South Africans thought differently, until now.

"When I started looking at death squads in 1989 I had no idea it was so widespread. I thought it was a limited manifestation of police brutality," said Jacques Pauw, whose acclaimed television documentary on de Kock's police hitsquad, shown last week, shocked the country.
His film, perhaps even more than the trial itself, has rammed home the message to anyone who still disbelieved the depths to which the white state sank in its twilight years.

Agents, freed in return for testifying against de Kock in court, told how they suffocated victims with rubber tubes, rammed burning sticks into their anuses, hung them up and beat them, and barbecued while bodies burned.
They claim South Africa's top police drank with them at their Vlakplaas base near Pretoria, and knew all about the dozens of people they killed.
Before now, there was enough room for doubt to comfort whites unwilling to believe what had been done on their behalf by leaders they voted for in ever greater numbers.
Evidence of a long-mooted death squad, full of soldiers hardened in wars in Angola and Rhodesia, surfaced in 1989 when de Kock's Vlakplaas predecessor Dirk Coetzee spoke up.

His superiors -- including a former police commissioner who last week told the "truth commission" that ex-president P.W. Botha personally ordered a civilian bombing -- denounced him as an agent of international communism.
A state commission, to which de Kock and his Vlakplaas cronies say they lied from start to finish, dismissed Coetzee's claims as baseless. Death squads did not exist.
Finally, the truth, or part of it, is out.

"White South Africa is beginning to emerge from a very long slumber," editor Battersby said. "Not even our wildest nightmares could have matched the horrifying reality of what was going on as we went about our 'normal' lives."
Liberals like him have urged fellow whites, few of whom admit these days to having backed apartheid, to assume collective guilt, even if they were unaware of the evils.

"People did not know because they did not want to know. Very much like what happened under the Nazi government in Germany," Pauw said. "It is very important that every white person takes responsibility for the actions of Eugene de Kock because he did it in our name."
But to other whites, more conservative, the proof of death squads changes little. They argue that there was a war going on in the 1980s, and neither side were angels.

"It's sick to believe there was a moral high ground when both sides were murdering on a grand scale," commentator Martin Williams wrote in the Citizen newspaper, rejecting the idea of collective guilt.
"I don't buy that for a host of personal reasons."
